name: Dorsal hump rasping (DIY)

lead: Dorsal hump rasping is the do-it-yourself attempt to flatten a bump on the bridge of the nose by filing or striking it. The payoff people want is a straighter, smoother side profile without paying for surgery.

The idea is that repeated filing or impact reduces the bone and cartilage of the bump. Reference sources describe hump reduction only as part of rhinoplasty, where a surgeon reshapes the bump with instruments under anesthesia and the nose is then taped and splinted while it heals. No published study or reliable source describes a home method, and the wiki's sources do not document how common it is.

paras: Posters who discuss it describe working on the bump themselves at home, without a surgeon. No published routine or timeline exists. The surgical version it imitates is followed by a dressing and splint, and swelling can take a year or more to settle fully.

The nasal bones and cartilage support breathing as well as shape. Injury, infection, airway problems and an uneven result are general concerns with any trauma to the nose, and no study evaluates the home practice. Anyone wanting a lower bridge can ask a facial plastic surgeon about rhinoplasty.

chain: Home filing or striking of bump
angle.text: The goal is a flatter, smoother nasal bridge without surgery. People who try it file or strike the bump at home, expecting the bone to wear down. Surgical sources describe hump reduction only as a surgeon-performed procedure.

lead: Dorsal hump rasping (DIY) is the name given to attempts to lower a bump on the nasal bridge at home by filing or striking it. The sources consulted for this wiki do not document how common the practice is or describe its methods.

In professional practice, reduction of a dorsal hump is part of rhinoplasty. After the surgeon reshapes the nose and closes incisions, the nose is dressed, taped and splinted to hold its position while it heals, and swelling can take at least a year to resolve fully [1].

paras: Rhinoplasty references describe surgeon-performed reshaping followed by taping and an external splint, with the dressing typically removed about a week after the operation [1]. Recovery involves prolonged swelling, and healing varies between individuals [1].
